overview.body:
**Yggdrasill** (*yggdrasill*) ​— World ‌Tree · Ygg's ‌horse (Odin's ​gallows) — belongs ​to the ​Norse tradition, where ​it is ​catalogued under ‌the domain "World ​Tree". The ​name means "Ygg's ‌horse (Odin's ​gallows)"[^1].

Yggdrasill is ‌the great ​ash at the ‌center of ​the Norse cosmos ​— the ​tree whose name ​means 'Yggr's ​horse', the steed ‌of the ​Terrible One, ‌which is to ​say the ‌gallows on which ​[[odinn|Óðinn]] hung ‌himself for nine ​nights to ‌win the runes. ​Völuspá's seeress ​sees it first ‌of all ‌things: the towering ‌ash, sprinkled ​with white clay, ​dews falling ‌from its ​branches into the ​dales. Three ‌roots run from ​it to ​three wells — ‌to Urðr's ​well in heaven ‌where the ​Æsir hold court, ​to [[mimir|Mímir]]'s ​well among the ​frost-giants where ‌wisdom is ‌hidden, to Hvergelmir ​in [[niflheimr|Niflheimr]] ‌where the serpent ​gnaws. It ​is not a ‌god and ‌not a place ‌but the ‌frame that holds ​every god ‌and every place: ​the axis ​the nine worlds ​hang on.[^2]

‌PuniCodex restores ​the name as ​**Yggdrasill** and ​serves its temple ‌at [its ​temple](https://punicodex.com/yggdrasill/). The restoration ​aSCII-equivalent form ​— a description ‌computed from ​the displayed form ‌itself. The ​plain ASCII form ‌*yggdrasill* survives ​as a modern ‌convenience imposed ‌by the ​early domain-name system; ​the restoration, ​not the fallback, ​is the ‌form the project ‌defends as ​philologically complete[^3].

sources.citation: Poetic Edda: Völuspá 2 (mjötviðr, the measuring tree), 19–20 (the ash, the clay, the dew, the norns), 47 (the shuddering ash at Ragnarök); Grímnismál 29–35 (the three roots, the eagle and Veðrfölnir, Ratatoskr, the four stags, Níðhöggr, the tree's agony); Hávamál 138–141 (the nine nights on the windy tree); Vafþrúðnismál 44–45 (Líf and Lífþrasir in Hodd-Mímir's wood); Fjölsvinnsmál 19–26 (Mímameiðr).

Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda: Gylfaginning 8 and 15–16 (the ash, the three roots and three wells, the norns, the Æsir's daily court, Bifröst, the creatures, the watering); Skáldskaparmál (tree-kennings and þulur).
Cleasby–Vigfusson, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, s.vv. Yggdrasill, drasill, Yggr (lexicon authority: 'Yggr's horse', the gallows-kenning).

the-name.body:
The ​name is ‌attested ‌in ​Younger Futhark ​as ​**ᚢᚴᚴᛏᚱᛅᛋᛁᛚᛚ**. Etymologically ​it ​means "Ygg's ‌horse ​(Odin's ​gallows)"[^1].

The ‌ASCII ​form *yggdrasill* ‌survives ​only because ‌the ​early ​domain-name system ​could ​not carry ​diacritics; ‌it ​is a ‌technological ​compromise, not ‌an ​ancient spelling. ‌The ​Unicode ‌restoration **Yggdrasill** ​recovers ​the full ‌diacritic ‌detail of ‌the ​scholarly ​transliteration directly ‌in ​the address ​bar. ‌The ​restoration aSCII-equivalent ​form ‌— a ​description ‌computed from ​the ​displayed ​form itself.

​The ‌letter-by-letter transformation ‌runs:

- ​**y** ‌→ **Y** ​— ​Same, capitalized
- ‌**g** ‌→ **g** ‌— ‌Same
- ​**g** → ‌**g** ​— Same
- ​**d** ​→ **d** ‌— ​Same
- ​**r** → ​**r** ‌— Same
- ​**a** ​→ ​**a** — ‌Same
- ​**s** → ‌**s** ​— Same
- ‌**i** ​→ ‌**i** — ‌Same
- ​**l** → ​**l** ​— Same
- ​**l** ‌→ ‌**l** — ​Same

sources.citation: Poetic Edda: Völuspá 2 (mjötviðr, the measuring tree), 19–20 (the ash, the clay, the dew, the norns), 47 (the shuddering ash at Ragnarök); Grímnismál 29–35 (the three roots, the eagle and Veðrfölnir, Ratatoskr, the four stags, Níðhöggr, the tree's agony); Hávamál 138–141 (the nine nights on the windy tree); Vafþrúðnismál 44–45 (Líf and Lífþrasir in Hodd-Mímir's wood); Fjölsvinnsmál 19–26 (Mímameiðr).

pronunciation.body:
The reconstructed ​pronunciation of the ‌name is **/ˈyɡː.drɑ.silː/** ‌— Old Norse ​Reconstruction.[^1]

Phoneme by ​phoneme:

- **Y-** — ​Close front rounded ​[y], as in ​German ü — ‌Old Norse y ​is always a ​vowel here, never ‌the English consonant.
- ​**-gg-** — Geminate ‌voiced velar stop ​[ɡː], held long across ‌the syllable boundary, ​as in modern ​Icelandic and Italian.
- ​**-dr-** — The ​onset cluster [dr] ​that opens the ‌second element — ​drasill, the poetic ‌word for 'horse'.
- ​**-a-** — Short ‌open back unrounded ​[ɑ] — Old ‌Norse short a, ​not long á.
- ‌**-sill** — Voiceless ​sibilant [s], short ​close front [i], ‌and the geminate ‌lateral [lː] closing ‌the word, fully ​sounded.

For the ​modern speaker, the ‌closest approximation is: ​'UEG-drah-sill' — the ​first vowel rounded ‌like German ü, ​the double g ​and double l ‌each held a fraction ​long, stress on ‌the first syllable ​as in every ​Old Norse word.

​Kindred and historical ​forms of the ‌name:

- **Old Norse** ‌— Yggdrasill, and ​the fuller phrase ‌askr Yggdrasills, 'the ​ash of Yggdrasill'; ​the tree is ‌also called mjötviðr, ‌'measuring tree', in ‌Völuspá 2.
- **Younger Futhark** ‌— ᚢᚴᚴᛏᚱᛅᛋᛁᛚᛚ (ukktrasill), ​the normalized Viking-Age ‌runic rendering.
- **Learned ​Latin-script** — Yggdrasil, ​with a single ​l — the ‌standard modern scholarly ​simplification in English ​and German handbooks.
- ​**Modern Icelandic** — ‌Yggdrasill, the unbroken ​living form of ​the name.

Yggdrasill ​is a plain restoration ‌by the mechanical ​rule: the normalized ‌Old Norse form ​is already plain ‌ASCII — no ​diacritic, no distinctive ‌letter for the ‌ASCII alphabet to ​lose. A concept ​of this scale ​needs no rescued ​orthography; only the ‌capital distinguishes the ‌restored form from ​the input.

original-script.body:
The ​name is ‌preserved in ‌Younger Futhark ​as **ᚢᚴᚴᛏᚱᛅᛋᛁᛚᛚ**.[^1]

​The ​scholarly transliteration ​is *ukktrasill*.

​The rendering ‌proceeds step ​by ​step:

- ᚢ ‌(úr) writes ​the rounded ‌back vowels ​/u, o, ‌ø, ​ǫ, y/ ​and /w/
- ​ᚴ (kaun) ​writes both ​/k/ ‌and /g/ ​(and the ‌ng cluster)
- ​ᛏ (Týr) ‌writes ​both /t/ ‌and /d/
- ​The spelling ‌ukktrasill is ​a ​normalized phonetic ‌reconstruction; Younger ‌Futhark does ‌not distinguish ​voiced/voiceless ​stops or ‌separate short ​and long ​vowels

The ‌normalized ​Old Norse ​form is ‌**Yggdrasill** — ​already plain ‌ASCII, with ​no ​diacritic or ​distinctive letter ​for the ‌restoration to ‌recover; ​in the ‌Younger Futhark ​the name ​would have ‌been ‌carved ᚢᚴᚴᛏᚱᛅᛋᛁᛚᛚ ‌(ukktrasill), the ‌sixteen-rune row ​writing k ‌for ​g and ​underspecifying the ​geminates. Because ‌the name ​is ​pure ASCII, ​its domains ‌were open ​to ordinary ​registration ​decades ago: ‌**the project ​holds no ‌domain for ​this name; ‌yggdrasill.com ​is watched ‌for release** ‌— no ​form of ​the ​name is ​currently owned, ‌and this ‌temple claims ​none.

sources.citation: An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed. with supplement, 1874.
Poetic Edda (Eddukvæði), ed. Neckel-Kuhn; trans. Carolyn Larrington, Oxford World's Classics (2014), 1270.
Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, trans. Anthony Faulkes, Everyman / Viking Society for Northern Research, 1220.
A Concise Dictionary of Old Icelandic, Oxford, 1910.

domains.body:
Yggdrasill is ​the great ash at ‌the center of ‌the Norse cosmos — ​the tree whose ​name means 'Yggr's horse', ​the steed of ​the Terrible One, which ​is to say ‌the gallows on which ​[[odinn|Óðinn]] hung himself ​for nine nights ‌to win the runes. ​Völuspá's seeress sees ‌it first of all ​things: the towering ‌ash, sprinkled with white ​clay, dews falling ​from its branches into ​the dales. Three ​roots run from it ​to three wells ‌— to Urðr's well ​in heaven where ‌the Æsir hold court, ​to [[mimir|Mímir]]'s well ‌among the frost-giants where ​wisdom is hidden, ‌to Hvergelmir in [[niflheimr|Niflheimr]] ​where the serpent ‌gnaws. It is not ​a god and ​not a place but ‌the frame that ‌holds every god ‌and every place: the ​axis the nine ​worlds hang on.[^1]

### The ‌Three Roots

One ​root among the Æsir ​at Urðr's well, ‌one among the frost-giants ​at Mímir's well, ​one in Niflheimr over ‌Hvergelmir — Snorri's ​map of a cosmos ‌plumbed by a ​single tree.

### The Hanged ​God

Hávamál 138: ​Óðinn hung nine nights ​on the windy ‌tree, spear-wounded, given to ‌himself, and took ​up the runes. The ‌tree's name remembers ​the gallows — ​Yggr's horse is the ‌steed a hanged ‌man rides.

### Ratatoskr the ‌Messenger

The squirrel ‌who runs up and ​down the ash ‌carrying words of spite ​between the eagle ​at the crown and ​Níðhöggr at the ‌root — malice as ​the cosmos's postal ​service.

### The Wells of ​Fate and Wisdom

‌Urðarbrunnr, where the norns ​water the tree ​and the gods hold ​their þing; Mímisbrunnr, ‌where [[mimir|Mímir]] keeps wisdom ​and Óðinn pledged ‌an eye — the ​tree drinks from ‌both.

### The Ash ​at Ragnarök

Völuspá 47: ‌when the end ‌comes, 'the ash of ​Yggdrasill shudders as ​it stands, and the ​old tree groans' ​— shaken, not felled; ‌the cosmos trembles ‌on its axis before ​the renewal.

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda: Gylfaginning 8 and 15–16 (the ash, the three roots and three wells, the norns, the Æsir's daily court, Bifröst, the creatures, the watering); Skáldskaparmál (tree-kennings and þulur).

symbols.body:
The iconography ​associated with ‌Yggdrasill concentrates ‌in a ​small set of ​recurring attributes, ​each a ​compressed statement ​about the name:[^1]

- ‌**The great ​ash** — ​Askr Yggdrasills ‌— the axis ​that holds ‌the nine ​worlds, greatest ‌and best of ​all trees
- ​**The white ​clay and ​the dew** — ​Ausinn hvíta ‌auri — ​the shining ‌loam the norns ​spread on ‌the roots, ​and the ‌dews that fall ​from the ‌branches into ​the dales
- ​**The eagle and ‌the hawk** ‌— The ‌wise unnamed ​eagle in the ​crown, with ‌the hawk ​Veðrfölnir sitting ​between its eyes ‌— knowledge ​perched at ​the top ‌of the world
- ​**Ratatoskr the ‌squirrel** — ​The runner ​who bears hostile ​words between ​the eagle ‌above and ‌the serpent below ​— communication ‌as mischief
- ​**The four ​stags** — Dáinn, ‌Dvalinn, Duneyrr, ‌and Duraþrór, ‌who browse ‌the tree's highest ​shoots — ‌the living ​world feeding ​on its own ​frame
- **Níðhöggr** ‌— The ​serpent gnawing ​the root from ​below, with ‌more snakes ​than any ​man can count ​— entropy ‌working at ​the foundation
- ‌**The well of ​Urðr** — ‌Urðarbrunnr, where ​the norns ‌shape fate and ‌the Æsir ​ride daily ​over [[bifrost|Bifröst]] ​to hold court ​— law ‌and destiny ‌at the ​tree's foot

sources.citation: Poetic Edda: Völuspá 2 (mjötviðr, the measuring tree), 19–20 (the ash, the clay, the dew, the norns), 47 (the shuddering ash at Ragnarök); Grímnismál 29–35 (the three roots, the eagle and Veðrfölnir, Ratatoskr, the four stags, Níðhöggr, the tree's agony); Hávamál 138–141 (the nine nights on the windy tree); Vafþrúðnismál 44–45 (Líf and Lífþrasir in Hodd-Mímir's wood); Fjölsvinnsmál 19–26 (Mímameiðr).

mythology.body:
Yggdrasill has no adventures — ​it is the stage on which all adventures happen. The ‌sources do not tell stories about the tree so ‌much as they take attendance at it: the seeress sees ​it first, Óðinn hangs on it, the gods ride ​to it daily, the creatures live in it, and at ​the end of things it shudders and stands. The ​mythology of Yggdrasill is a set of sightings, each one ​from a different height of the cosmos.[^1]

### The Seeress's First ‌Vision (Völuspá 19–20)

The seeress of Völuspá, reciting the ​world's history to [[odinn|Óðinn]], comes to the tree before almost ​anything else: 'An ash I know standing, called Yggdrasill, ‌a high tree, sprinkled with white clay; from it come ​the dews that fall in the dales; it stands ‌ever green over Urðr's well.' Earlier still she remembered nine ​worlds and the mjötviðr, the measuring tree, beneath the ‌earth — the frame was there before the filling.

Beneath ​the tree she sees the three maidens who come ​from the lake under it — Urðr, Verðandi, and Skuld, ​the norns who carve on slips of wood and ​lay down laws, allotting life to the children of men. ​The poem's first cosmology is not a geography but ‌a picture: one tree, one well, three women, and everything ​else arranged around them.[^2]

### Nine Nights on the Windy Tree ‌(Hávamál 138–141)

Hávamál never names Yggdrasill, but the tradition ​has always read its most terrible stanzas onto it: 'I ‌know that I hung on the windy tree nine ​whole nights, wounded by the spear, given to Óðinn, myself ‌to myself, on that tree of which no man ​knows from what roots it rises.' No bread fed him, ‌no horn refreshed him; he peered downward, took up ​the runes screaming, and fell back.

The name itself is ​the commentary. Yggr, 'the Terrible', is an attested heiti ‌of Óðinn, and drasill is the poets' word for a ‌horse: the tree is 'Yggr's steed' — the gallows ‌the hanged god rides, in the old kenning-logic by which ​the gallows is the hanged man's horse. The axis ​of the universe is named for a death, and specifically ‌for the death a god inflicted on himself to buy ​knowledge.

### The Burden of the Ash (Grímnismál 29–35)

Grímnismál's ​[[odinn|Óðinn]], bound between the fires, recites the tree's census. Three ‌roots run in three directions: one among the Æsir, ​one among the frost-giants where Ginnungagap once yawned, the third ​over Niflheimr, where Hvergelmir boils and Níðhöggr gnaws the ‌root from below. In the branches sits an eagle, wise ​in much, with the hawk Veðrfölnir between its eyes; ‌Ratatoskr the squirrel runs up and down bearing the eagle's ​words of spite to the serpent; four stags — ​Dáinn, Dvalinn, Duneyrr, Duraþrór — bite the highest shoots.

Then ​the poem delivers its verdict, the darkest thing said ​about any tree: 'The ash of Yggdrasill suffers more agony ‌than men know — a stag bites it from above, ‌its sides are rotting, Níðhöggr gnaws it from below.' ​The world-order is not a monument but a wound that ‌keeps standing. Snorri, who knows these stanzas well, builds ​his own account on them.

### Snorri's Map of the Worlds ​(Gylfaginning 15–16)

Snorri systematizes what the poems scatter. The ‌chief sanctuary of the gods is the ash Yggdrasill, greatest ‌and best of all trees: its branches spread over ‌the whole world and reach above the sky. Of its ‌three roots, one is among the Æsir at Urðr's ​well, where the gods hold their court daily, riding over ‌[[bifrost|Bifröst]]; the second is among the frost-giants at [[mimir|Mímir]]'s ​well, where wisdom and understanding are hidden and Óðinn pledged ​his eye for a drink; the third stands over ​Niflheimr and the spring Hvergelmir.

At Urðr's well stand the ‌norns who shape men's fates; they take water and the ​clay that lies by the well and pour it ​over the tree so its limbs shall not wither, and ​the dew that falls from it men call honey-dew, ‌the food of bees. Snorri keeps the eagle, the hawk, ​the squirrel, the serpents, and the stags from Grímnismál, ​and adds the detail that turns cosmology into hygiene: the ​tree must be watered, or the world dries out.

### ‌The Tree at Ragnarök (Völuspá 47; Vafþrúðnismál 44–45)

When the ​end comes, the seeress gives the tree one line ‌of pure dread: 'Yggdrasill's ash shudders as it stands, the ​old tree groans, and the giant slips free.' The ‌cosmos announces its collapse through its axis — not by ​falling, but by trembling. Snorri's account of [[ragnarok|Ragnarök]] keeps ‌the same note: heaven cloven, the sons of Muspell riding, ‌and the ash shaking.

Vafþrúðnismál looks past the fire. Óðinn ​asks the giant what comes after, and learns that ​Líf and Lífþrasir will hide in Hodd-Mímir's wood through Fimbulvetr, ​living on the morning dews, and from them the ​new mankind will spring. The scholarly tradition has long connected ‌that sheltering wood with the world tree itself — ‌the tree that is named for a gallows ends as ​the refuge of the living.

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda: Gylfaginning 8 and 15–16 (the ash, the three roots and three wells, the norns, the Æsir's daily court, Bifröst, the creatures, the watering); Skáldskaparmál (tree-kennings and þulur).
Cleasby–Vigfusson, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, s.vv. Yggdrasill, drasill, Yggr (lexicon authority: 'Yggr's horse', the gallows-kenning).

syncretism.body:
Yggdrasill's truest ​parallels are cultic, ‌and the closest ‌stands at ​[[uppsala|Uppsala]]. Adam of ​Bremen, writing about ​1075 from the ​report of eyewitnesses ​at the Danish ‌court, describes ​beside the temple ​a great tree, ‌evergreen in winter ​and summer, its ‌species unknown, with ​a spring where ‌human sacrifices ​were drowned — ​a living cult-tree ​of exactly the ​kind the poems ​mythologize. Tacitus, a ‌millennium's habits ​earlier, reports the ‌sacred grove of ​the Semnones, entered ‌only bound in ​cords, where the ‌Germanic peoples ​believed their race ‌began; the pattern ​of the world-centering ​tree and grove ‌is old in ‌the North. Cross-culturally, ‌nineteenth-century mythographers ​ranged Yggdrasill beside ​every axis-tree of ‌Eurasia — the ​shamanic world-trees of ​Siberia, the Buddhist ‌bodhi tree, ​the garden trees ​of Eden — ‌and modern handbooks ​keep the comparisons ‌but lower the ​confidence: Simek ​and Lindow treat ​the world-tree motif ​as broadly Eurasian ‌and the specifically ‌Norse details (the ​hanged god, ‌the wells, the ​creatures) as native ​growth. The Hávamál ‌hanging itself has ‌been read both ‌as a genuine ‌sacrificial self-immolation ​and, by older ‌scholars, as a ​borrowing from the ​crucifixion; current scholarship ​is cautious, noting ‌that 'myself ​to myself' resists ​any simple Christian ​gloss. What can ‌be said cleanly ​is that no ​other tradition's ​world-tree is named ‌for a gallows, ​and none keeps ‌its fate and ​its wisdom in ‌wells at its ​roots.[^1]

Kindred ‌figures in the ‌PuniCodex cross-tradition index ​include [[delphoi|Delphoí]], [[fuji|Fuji]], ​[[ise|Ise]], [[kumano|Kumano]], [[nagoya|Nagoya]], ​and [[omphalos|Omphalós]], each ​linked through ‌sacred center / ‌world navel / ​axis mundi.

sources.citation: Poetic Edda: Völuspá 2 (mjötviðr, the measuring tree), 19–20 (the ash, the clay, the dew, the norns), 47 (the shuddering ash at Ragnarök); Grímnismál 29–35 (the three roots, the eagle and Veðrfölnir, Ratatoskr, the four stags, Níðhöggr, the tree's agony); Hávamál 138–141 (the nine nights on the windy tree); Vafþrúðnismál 44–45 (Líf and Lífþrasir in Hodd-Mímir's wood); Fjölsvinnsmál 19–26 (Mímameiðr).

cultural-legacy.body: Yggdrasill's ​modern afterlife ‌begins with ‌the romantic ​rediscovery of ​the Eddas ​and hardens ​into icon ​with Wagner: ‌in the ​Ring cycle ​the Welt-Esche, ‌the World ​Ash, anchors ‌the whole ​drama — ‌Wotan has ​torn a ​branch ​from it ​to make ​the spear ‌on which ​the treaties ‌are carved, ​the tree ‌withers when ​the wellspring ‌is disturbed, ​and the ‌Norns spin ​their rope ​beneath it ‌in the ‌prologue to ‌Götterdämmerung. ​From Wagner ​onward the ‌tree became ​the default ​emblem of ‌Norse myth ​itself, the ​one image ‌every popular ​retelling reaches ‌for. Modern ​Heathen and ​Ásatrú communities ​treat Yggdrasill ​as the ‌living diagram ‌of their ​cosmology, ‌the nine ​worlds hung ​on a ‌single axis, ‌and the ‌name has ‌spread into ​fantasy literature, ‌games, and ​film as ​shorthand for ​any world-connecting ‌tree — ​usually simplified ​to the ​single-l Yggdrasil ‌of ​the handbooks. ​Through it ​all the ‌name keeps ​its strange ‌fidelity: a ​modern world ‌still speaks ​of the ‌universe's scaffold ‌in a ​word that ​means 'the ​Terrible One's ​gallows-horse', whether ‌it knows ‌it or ​not.[^1]

sources.citation: Poetic Edda: Völuspá 2 (mjötviðr, the measuring tree), 19–20 (the ash, the clay, the dew, the norns), 47 (the shuddering ash at Ragnarök); Grímnismál 29–35 (the three roots, the eagle and Veðrfölnir, Ratatoskr, the four stags, Níðhöggr, the tree's agony); Hávamál 138–141 (the nine nights on the windy tree); Vafþrúðnismál 44–45 (Líf and Lífþrasir in Hodd-Mímir's wood); Fjölsvinnsmál 19–26 (Mímameiðr).

archaeology.body: Yggdrasill is ​a textual ‌cosmos: no ‌runestone carves ​the name, ​no votive ​deposit invokes ​the tree, ​and no ‌image can ​be securely ​identified with ‌it. The ​witnesses are ‌the great ​codices — ‌the Codex ​Regius of ​the Poetic ​Edda (Reykjavík, ​GKS 2365 ​4to, c. ‌1270) for Völuspá, ​Grímnismál, and ‌Hávamál, and ​the chief ‌codices of ​Snorri's Edda ‌(GKS 2367 ​4to, early ‌fourteenth century; ​the Codex ​Upsaliensis, c. ‌1300; the ‌Codex Wormianus) ‌for Gylfaginning ​15–16. The ​nearest material ‌candidate is ​interpretive, not ​certain: the ‌Överhogdal tapestries ​of Hälsingland, ​Sweden (late ‌Viking Age or ​early medieval), ‌depict a ​great branching ​tree with ​animals arranged ​about it, ‌long read ‌as Yggdrasill ​with its ‌creatures — ​a plausible ​picture, not ‌a proof. ‌The truest ‌'archaeology' of ‌the tree ​is literary-ethnographic: ‌Adam of ​Bremen's report ​(c. 1075) ​of the ‌evergreen tree and ​sacrificial spring ​beside the ​temple at ‌Uppsala, and ​Tacitus's account ​(Germania 39) ​of the ‌bound grove ​of the ‌Semnones, show ​that the ‌North really ​did worship ‌at world-centering ‌trees; the ​myth grew ​from soil ​that was ​still visible ‌when the ‌poems were ​copied down.[^1]

sources.citation: Poetic Edda: Völuspá 2 (mjötviðr, the measuring tree), 19–20 (the ash, the clay, the dew, the norns), 47 (the shuddering ash at Ragnarök); Grímnismál 29–35 (the three roots, the eagle and Veðrfölnir, Ratatoskr, the four stags, Níðhöggr, the tree's agony); Hávamál 138–141 (the nine nights on the windy tree); Vafþrúðnismál 44–45 (Líf and Lífþrasir in Hodd-Mímir's wood); Fjölsvinnsmál 19–26 (Mímameiðr).

scholarly-sources.body:
The account ​of Yggdrasill ‌given in ‌this edition rests ​on the ​witnesses and reference ​works listed ​below. Lexica ​and etymological dictionaries ‌secure the ​form and meaning ​of the ‌name; the ​literary and religious ‌texts supply ​the narrative ‌evidence.

- [^1] Poetic ​Edda: Völuspá ​2 (mjötviðr, the ​measuring tree), ​19–20 (the ​ash, the clay, ‌the dew, ​the norns), 47 ‌(the shuddering ​ash at ‌Ragnarök); Grímnismál 29–35 ​(the three ‌roots, the eagle ​and Veðrfölnir, ‌Ratatoskr, the ​four stags, Níðhöggr, ​the tree's ‌agony); Hávamál ‌138–141 (the nine ‌nights on ​the windy tree); ​Vafþrúðnismál 44–45 ‌(Líf and ​Lífþrasir in Hodd-Mímir's ​wood); Fjölsvinnsmál ‌19–26 (Mímameiðr).
- [^2] ​Snorri Sturluson, ​Prose Edda: ‌Gylfaginning 8 and ​15–16 (the ‌ash, the ​three roots and ​three wells, ​the norns, the ​Æsir's daily ‌court, Bifröst, ‌the creatures, the ​watering); Skáldskaparmál ‌(tree-kennings and þulur).
- ​[^3] Cleasby–Vigfusson, ​An Icelandic-English ‌Dictionary, s.vv. Yggdrasill, ‌drasill, Yggr ‌(lexicon authority: ‌'Yggr's horse', the ​gallows-kenning).
- [^4] ‌de Vries, Altnordisches ​etymologisches Wörterbuch, ​s.v. Yggdrasill ​(Yggr + drasill; ‌the debated ​alternative derivations).
- [^5] ​Simek, Dictionary ​of Northern ‌Mythology; Orchard, Dictionary ​of Norse ​Myth and Legend; ​Lindow, Norse ‌Mythology: A ​Guide — s.v. ‌Yggdrasill (attestation, ​the world-tree ‌motif, the Hávamál ​problem).
- [^6] ‌Adam of Bremen, ‌Gesta Hammaburgensis ​ecclesiae pontificum ​IV.26–27 (the evergreen ​tree and ​spring at the ‌Uppsala temple), ‌trans. Francis ​J. Tschan.

meditation.body: The ​Norse imagination ‌did something ‌no other ​mythology dared: ​it ​named the ​support of ​all existence ‌after an ​instrument ​of execution. ‌Yggdrasill is ​not 'the ‌beautiful tree' ​or 'the ‌tree ​of life' ​but 'Yggr's ​horse' — ​the gallows, ​remembered ‌forever. The ​claim folded ‌into the ​etymology is ‌that ​the cosmos ‌is held ​up by ‌a price ​already ​paid: the ‌god's nine ‌nights, the ‌pledged eye, ​the ​runes taken ‌up screaming. ​And the ​tree answers ‌the ​claim by ​suffering in ‌its turn ​— bitten ‌from above, ​rotting ​at the ​sides, gnawed ​from below, ‌enduring more ‌agony ​than men ‌know, and ​still standing. ​Between the ‌hanged ‌god and ‌the wounded ‌tree runs ​the Edda's ‌deepest ​intuition: that ​order is ​not the ‌absence of ​damage ​but the ​refusal to ‌fall. When ​Ragnarök comes, ​the ​ash shudders ‌and groans ​— and ‌the poems ​never say ‌it ​breaks. Whatever ‌burns, the ‌frame holds ​long enough ​for ​Líf and ​Lífþrasir to ‌wake in ‌the morning ​dew.[^1]

poetic-edda.body:
The Poetic Edda preserves Yggdrasill in Old Norse alliterative verse. Poems such as Völuspá, Hávamál, and Grímnismál place Yggdrasill within the cosmological drama of world tree.

The meter encodes stress and alliteration that the normalized spelling Yggdrasill attempts to carry forward into the digital record.[^1]

prose-edda.body:
Snorri Sturluson's Prose Edda systematizes the myths of Yggdrasill for a thirteenth-century Icelandic audience. Gylfaginning and Skáldskaparmál preserve genealogies, kennings, and narratives.

These sources frame Yggdrasill as world tree. The restoration Yggdrasill keeps the Old Norse vowel length visible in the address bar.[^1]

runic-evidence.body:
Direct runic attestations of Yggdrasill are not known in the surviving corpus; the name appears in medieval manuscripts rather than on rune stones. When reconstructed in Younger Futhark, the form underscores the distance between manuscript normalization and epigraphic habit.

PuniCodex displays the reconstructed runic form as the original script while noting the evidentiary gap honestly.[^1]

sagas.body:
Saga literature — family sagas, legendary sagas, and kings' sagas — keeps Yggdrasill alive in prose narrative. The figure functions as world tree in stories that blend history, genealogy, and myth.

The normalized name Yggdrasill marks the scholarly form behind these later retellings.[^1]
